Provide examples of global sparsity levels at which this empirical convergence occurs: the authors examined multiple global sparsity levels (figures and text reference "36%", "64%"/"67%", and "83%") and observed the near-identical layerwise patterns persist across these multiple global sparsity settings, demonstrating the convergence is not limited to a single sparsity regime.
Figure 8

Conclude that the per-layer sparsity allocations discovered by different magnitude-based pruning approaches (IMP, OMP, GMP) are strikingly similar and in many experiments almost identical across encoder layers, with notable differences primarily in very deep layers such as classification heads; this empirical convergence of layerwise sparsities holds across commonsense, arithmetic, and other SMC-Bench settings and occurs at multiple global sparsity levels.

Begin from the empirical result that magnitude-based pruning approaches produce nearly identical layerwise sparsity patterns (conclusion 6) and recall the authors' investigation intent to explain why common pruning heuristics fail on SMC-Bench.

Define the "lazy regime" as the authors use the term: a training or fine-tuning regime in which an overparameterized model's weights change very little from their pre-trained initialization during downstream fine-tuning, so that the model essentially stays in the same loss basin and parameter updates are small; cite the theoretical/empirical references the authors invoked to motivate this concept.
Chizat et al., 2019; Malladi et al., 2022

Explain the authors' reasoning that connects the observed near-identical layerwise sparsity patterns to the lazy regime: because weights change negligibly during fine-tuning in this regime, simple pruning criteria based on weight magnitude or gradient become less informative (their signals do not meaningfully distinguish important from unimportant parameters), and hence different magnitude-based methods that rely on those criteria (before, during, or after fine-tuning) tend to collapse to the same layerwise sparsity solution (the authors explicitly state that the observed collapse "reminds us of the 'lazy training' regime" and that "weights of RoBERTa excluding classifiers remain rather stable during commonsense reasoning fine-tuning").
Figure 6

State the implication drawn by the authors: because magnitude and gradient-based pruning criteria become noisy or uninformative in the lazy regime, these commonly used heuristics are unreliable for identifying subnetworks that preserve dense performance on SMC-Bench; this unreliability helps explain the widespread failures of standard pruning heuristics observed empirically across the benchmark.

Start from the established explanation that magnitude/gradient signals are unreliable in the lazy regime (conclusion 7) and note the authors' hypothesis that second-order pruning approaches, which use curvature (Hessian) information, should provide more faithful pruning signals under these conditions.
Kurtic et al., 2022

Define the second-order pruning framework evaluated by the authors: "oBERT" denotes the authors' adopted second-order pruning approach that approximates inverse-Hessian information to score parameters for pruning; define "LRR" as Learning Rate Rewinding (rewinding learning rates during pruning iterations) and "KD" as Knowledge Distillation (using a teacher model's outputs to guide the student) which the authors incorporated into their stronger pruning recipe; also state the authors' additional recipe choices: keeping embeddings and classification heads dense during pruning.
Renda et al., 2020; Hinton et al., 2015

Describe the experimental implementation used by the authors to test the hypothesis: on RoBERTa-Large for CSQA they replaced the magnitude criterion in an LTH-style iterative pruning framework with the oBERT second-order criterion, applied Learning Rate Rewinding and Knowledge Distillation during each pruning iteration, and kept embeddings and classification heads dense; the authors then compared resulting accuracies and layerwise sparsity patterns against zero- and first-order sparsification methods.
Figure 9

Present the empirical outcome: the authors report that oBERT combined with LRR and KD "notably outperforms the zero-order and first-order sparsification approaches" on CSQA and substantially improves accuracy to a competitive level; additionally, oBERT yields a qualitatively different layerwise sparsity pattern (more typical of computer-vision-style patterns where deeper layers have higher sparsities), showing that second-order information leads to different pruning allocations that better preserve performance.
Figure 9
Figure 10

Report the authors' characterization of costs and remaining gaps: the authors state that this improved recipe is resource-intensive—reporting roughly a $9\times$ increase in fine-tuning time relative to baseline fine-tuning when using the oBERT+LRR+KD pipeline (the paper explicitly states "9× more fine‑tuning time" in the investigation), and that despite improved performance the best sparse models still trail the dense baseline by an approximate $\sim 10\%$ accuracy gap at global sparsities in the 60%–80% range.
Figure 9

Conclude that replacing zero- or first-order pruning criteria with a second-order framework (oBERT) and combining it with stronger recipes (LRR and KD, and keeping embeddings and classification heads dense) substantially improves pruning outcomes on SMC-Bench and produces qualitatively different, more favorable layerwise sparsity patterns, but at the expense of substantially higher computational cost (reported ~9× fine-tuning time) and with a remaining ~10% accuracy gap relative to dense models at high sparsities.

Begin from the SMC-Bench evaluations (conclusion 1) and the authors' layerwise analyses (conclusion 6 and C.1): define "layer collapse" as the situation where pruning removes nearly all parameters from a layer (particularly non-embedding layers), causing severe blockage of signal propagation and catastrophic performance loss.

Provide the authors' empirical assertion that layer collapse is not ubiquitous across pruning methods on SMC-Bench: the authors report that they did not observe severe layer collapse across methods except for specific cases; they explicitly single out SNIP and OMP (Before) as methods that cause collapse in particular settings.

Give the evidence for SNIP-induced collapse: the authors show in their layerwise-sparsity plots that SNIP aggressively prunes embedding layers, reaching approximately 99% or higher embedding sparsity even at mild global sparsities (for example, SNIP prunes embedding layers to ~99.7% at a reported global sparsity of 36%), which is presented as an instance of severe collapse specific to SNIP and explains SNIP's poor downstream results.
Figure 6

Give the evidence for OMP (Before)-induced collapse in arithmetic models: the authors report in Appendix B that Magnitude Before Training (OMP (Before)) dramatically reduces accuracy to nearly zero when global sparsity exceeds 36% in arithmetic reasoning experiments and that analysis of layerwise sparsities shows OMP (Before) completely empties non-embedding deep layers under these sparsity conditions, which they attribute to layer collapse.
Appendix B

Provide the additional empirical evidence in protein models showing that even small module-wise pruning can measurably harm performance: the authors performed OMP (After) pruning of 5% of weights in various modules of ESM-1B (Q, K, V, O, and FFN) on the HP-S²C2 dataset and report the dense accuracy of 94.68 dropping to 92.19 when those modules are pruned by 5%, which demonstrates that small module-wise pruning can still significantly degrade protein thermostability prediction accuracy and indicates low parameter redundancy in some pre-trained protein backbones for these tasks.
Table 1

Conclude that severe layer collapse is not a universal outcome across pruning methods on SMC-Bench, but it does occur for particular pruning choices—SNIP aggressively removing embedding weights and OMP (Before) emptying non-embedding deep layers in arithmetic models—and that small, module-wise pruning in protein models can measurably harm accuracy (e.g., ESM-1B accuracy 94.68 → 92.19 when pruning Q,K,V,O,FFN by 5%), supporting the authors' claim about targeted collapse and low redundancy in some modules.

open_questions.content: The paper explicitly acknowledges and documents several unresolved scientific and engineering challenges for sparse neural networks when applied to the SMC‑Bench regime: (1) designing sparse training and pruning algorithms that are both computationally efficient and reliably preserve dense performance on challenging downstream tasks remains open—second‑order methods improve accuracy but are currently too expensive and still do not fully close the gap; (2) formulating pruning criteria that remain informative in the “lazy regime” of fine‑tuning large pre‑trained models (i.e., criteria that do not collapse to identical per‑layer patterns and that avoid pruning critical modules such as embeddings) is unresolved; (3) understanding and characterizing domain‑dependent parameter redundancy (e.g., why protein backbones like ESM‑1B show low tolerance even to small module‑wise pruning) requires further study; and (4) developing sparsification pipelines that generalize across diverse modalities and task difficulties (so that prior‑training, during‑training, and post‑training methods are robustly applicable without extensive manual tuning such as LRR and KD) is left as future work by the authors.
